## Overview

The Molala are a Native American people of Oregon whose traditional territory extended across the Western Cascades, from Mount Hood and the Molalla River to the headwaters of the Rogue River. Their descendants reside among the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community of Oregon, Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians, and the Klamath Tribes. In the 1950s, 141 of the 882 Grand Ronde Reservation members claimed Molala descent. Molala society was organized around winter villages and seasonal movement to food resources, while leadership was decentralized and associated with assistance to relatives. The Molala language is extinct and is included in the Plateau Penutian language family; Klamath and Sahaptin are considered its closest related languages. Although few recorded sources exist, Molala material, linguistic, historical, and mythological records document a distinct culture of hunting, fishing, gathering, craft production, and storytelling.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They record that animal hides were a source of wealth and that Molala produced beaded moccasins and woven baskets. Henry Yelkes was described wearing a hat of deerskin and flicker feathers that had belonged to his grandfather.

### Architecture

Molala society centered on winter villages, usually occupied by a single extended family in low-elevation locations. Winter homesteads were semi-subterranean and made from red cedar and western hemlock planks. Summer homes were unexcavated and made of thatch or bark.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They record composite bows made from Pacific Yew and sinew, bows and arrows used in hunting, basket traps and harpoons used to capture fish, and a private collection in Mt Angel containing 535 flint arrowheads, an 8-inch tomahawk head, and beadwork. Animal hides and dentalium crafts were among the primary sources of wealth. Canoes made by Upper Chinookans were particularly sought after by the Northern Molala.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They mention dentalium crafts as a source of wealth, beadwork in a private collection of Molala artifacts, and an exchange in which the Southern Molala traded buckskins for Klamath beads and wocus seeds.

## Music & performance

They do record oral narratives collected by ethnographers, including stories told by the Molala about the world being covered in water and about the creation of the Molala people. Stephen Savage told the latter story to Albert S. Gatschet in 1877. The sources also identify Molala Kate Chantal as an ethnographic informant and Victoria Wishikin Howard as a storyteller. No musical tradition is described in the available material.

## Dance & theatre

The available material refers to myths, ethnographic texts, and storytelling.

## Festivals & rituals

They state that seasonal resources shaped social organization: when resources became available, families separated into smaller groups to exploit and gather them. The sources describe hunting, fishing, and gathering as recurring seasonal activities. Camas bulbs were gathered in western prairies; hazelnuts and tarweed seeds were collected in summer and autumn; Mountain Huckleberries and other berries were collected in the late summer. These seasonal movements are documented, but no named festival or ritual calendar is given.

The historical record includes treaty negotiations and reservation relocations rather than ceremonial observances. On 6 May, the Northern Molala agreed to payments of goods, cash, and a reservation centered on the Molalla River; on the following day, the Upper Santiam Molala agreed to similar terms. During the winter of 1855–1856, the Northern Molala and Upper Santiam Molala were forced to relocate to the Grand Ronde Reservation.

## Foodways

Molala foodways depended on hunting, fishing, and seasonal plant gathering. Roosevelt elk and Black-tailed deer were described as the economically most important resources. Big game was hunted mainly with bow and arrow, while pitfalls, snares, and hunting dogs were also used. Steelhead and Chinook salmon were captured with basket traps or harpoons; the meat was dried and stored for future consumption.

Camas bulbs were an important caloric resource in western prairies. They were baked in earth ovens, dried, blended with hazelnuts, and stored in sacks. Hazelnuts and tarweed seeds were gathered in summer and autumn. In the higher elevations of the Cascades, Mountain Huckleberries, Cascade Blueberry, Oval-leaf Huckleberry, and Red Huckleberry were collected in the late summer and dried. Huckleberry Mountain, near Crater Lake, was the single-most important berry-gathering area for the Southern Molala and Klamath. Other recorded berries include Littleleaf Huckleberry, Western Blueberry, Manzanita Berry, Wild Strawberry, Black Twinberry, Evergreen Blackberry, Blackcap Raspberry, Thimbleberry, Blue Elderberry, Red Elderberry, Wax Currant, and Rose hips from the local Wild Rose.

## Oral tradition & literature

Only a few Molala myths remain extant, and they were recorded by ethnographers in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Franz Boas recorded a story in which the world was once entirely covered in water; as the water receded, Mount Hood became exposed first and later the Willamette Valley.

A prominent creation story was told by Stephen Savage to Albert S. Gatschet in 1877. Near Mount Hood, Coyote encountered Grizzly Bear, who challenged Coyote to a duel. Coyote proposed a contest to see who could eat the most hot stones, but Coyote ate wild strawberries instead. After Grizzly Bear died, Coyote scattered the body in pieces and threw the heart to the Molala country, declaring that the Molala would be good hunters and would think continually about hunting deer.

The sources identify manuscripts containing “Marriage Ceremonies,” “Myth or the Coyote,” and “Molale tribe raided by the Cayuse.” They also record Victoria Wishikin Howard as a storyteller and Molala Kate Chantal as an ethnographic informant and among the last speakers of Molala.

## Language & religion

Molala is an extinct language once spoken by the Molala people of Oregon. It is included in the Plateau Penutian language family, with Klamath and Sahaptin considered the closest related languages. Three dialects are recorded: Northern Molala, spoken in the Molalla River watershed; Upper Santiam Molala, spoken along the upper Santiam River; and Southern Molala, spoken along the headwaters of the Umpqua and Rogue rivers.

The sources describe Molala as a verb-heavy polysynthetic language with seven cases: nominative, accusative, genitive, instrumental, locative, allative, and ablative. They do document myths involving Coyote, Grizzly Bear, the origin of the world, and the creation of the Molala people.
